summary: A document from the Network Graphics Group describing part of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol for sending graphics from a serving host to a display package at a using host. The protocol was a stream of 8-bit bytes called the graphics output byte stream. It reflects decisions from a late-1971 meeting and obsoletes RFC 292.

eli5.summary: Rules for sending pictures from one computer to another's screen as a long series of small numbers that the screen turns into drawings.

questions: what is the arpanet graphics protocol
what are the graphics protocol levels
how did early arpanet send graphics
subtitle: A proposed ARPANET protocol for sending drawing commands as a byte stream to a remote display.

tldr.problem: A program at one host (the Serving Host) needed a standard way to draw pictures on a graphics console at another host (the Using Host).
tldr.mechanism: The protocol defines a graphics output byte stream of 8-bit bytes. Commands sit in numbered levels, from level 0 (move, draw, dot, text) up to subpictures and viewports, and they use a logical coordinate system that each display maps to its own screen.
tldr.outcome: The document is explicitly a basis for discussion and experimentation. It obsoletes RFC 292, covers only output to the display, and warns that command codes might be reassigned.

today: RFC 493 obsoletes RFC 292, and its status is recorded as Unknown. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it, and the text itself calls the protocol proposed and experimental.

sections.title: Scope of the Proposal
sections.content:
This RFC reflects decisions from the second meeting of the Network Graphics Group at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in late November 1971. It describes part of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol: the form and content of graphics data sent from the Serving Host to a display package at the Using Host, called the graphics output byte stream.

It does not cover graphics input, nor how the connection between hosts is established (the Connection Committee's job). It also notes that no facility lets the Using Host report logical errors in the stream back to the Serving Host.
sections.eli5: This note only explains how to send drawing instructions one way, from the computer making the picture to the computer showing it.

sections.title: Levels, Data Forms and Coordinates
sections.content:
Functions are grouped into levels. A host claiming level N must implement all lower levels, and level N needs no knowledge of level N+1. A valid stream at level K should produce identical results on any interpreter of level K or higher.

A command is a command byte followed by zero or more arguments. A value is an 8-bit integer, and a string is a count followed by that many bytes (a count from 0 to 127 fits in one byte, larger ones use two). Coordinates use a two-dimensional logical system: two's complement fractions, with each screen edge of unit length and the origin at the screen center, so values run from -1/2 to just under +1/2. Two bytes per coordinate were decided to suffice for now. Text uses Network ASCII.
sections.eli5: The instructions come in steps of difficulty. A simple screen only has to know the easy ones, and a fancier screen can learn the harder ones later without breaking the easy ones.

sections.title: Level 0 Commands
sections.content:
Level 0 is kept very simple so that even the least powerful host or a programmable terminal can implement it. A command is included only if its output depends solely on the command and the current beam position, so no stored modes or stacks are needed. The commands are numbered 0 to 11: Null, Erase screen and reset beam, Move, Draw, Dot (each in absolute and relative forms), Text, TextR, End of Picture and Escape to device specifics.

Bits 4, 2 and 1 of the opcode have special meaning for move, line and dot: the 1 bit selects absolute or relative data, the 4 bit whether any visible output occurs, and the 2 bit whether the output is a line or a dot. ERASE announces a new picture and must be paired with ENDPIC. TEXTR restores the beam after displaying text, and the RFC discourages plain TEXT.
sections.eli5: The simplest set has just a few moves: pick up the pen and move it, draw a line, put a dot, write some words, and start a fresh page.

sections.title: Higher Levels: Subpictures and Viewports
sections.content:
Level 1 adds line mode (solid, dashed, dotted), intensity, formatted text and subpictures, which are named pictures defined once and then called. Level 2 adds a pushdown stack of saved beam positions (mark) and arbitrary levels of simple subpicture calls. Level 3 adds full subpicture calls that can translate, rotate, scale or apply an affine transformation, and level 4 adds viewports, rectangles of the logical screen in which subpictures are shown.

The document also leaves some behavior explicitly unspecified, such as what happens when a line is drawn beyond the screen edge, and it advises implementers to allow for command codes being reassigned.
sections.eli5: Later levels let you save a small drawing, like a house, and stamp it many times, bigger, smaller or turned around. They also let you split the screen into windows.

items.label: Erase screen and reset beam
items.desc: Starts a new picture; paired with End of Picture.

items.label: Move Absolute
items.desc: Move the beam invisibly to an x,y position.

items.label: Move Relative
items.desc: Move the beam invisibly by an x,y amount.

items.label: Draw Absolute
items.desc: Draw a line to an absolute x,y position.

items.label: Draw Relative
items.desc: Draw a line by an x,y amount from the beam position.

items.label: Dot Absolute
items.desc: Move to x,y and display a dot.

items.label: Dot Relative
items.desc: Move by an x,y amount and display a dot.

items.label: Text
items.desc: Display a string at the beam position; discouraged in favor of TextR.

items.label: TextR
items.desc: Display a string, then restore the beam position.

items.label: End of Picture
items.desc: Ends a picture started with Erase.

items.label: Escape
items.desc: Pass device-specific bytes through to one device.
